text: Gradient descent minimizes a loss function by repeatedly moving the model parameters in the direction opposite to the gradient. Each step is scaled by the learning rate.
The learning rate controls the step size of optimization. If it is too large training diverges or oscillates, and if it is too small convergence is very slow.
Batch normalization normalizes layer activations using the mean and variance of each mini-batch, which stabilizes training and allows higher learning rates.
Dropout randomly switches off a fraction of neurons during training so the network cannot rely on any single unit, which reduces overfitting.
A random forest trains many decision trees on bootstrapped samples with random feature subsets and averages their votes, which lowers variance compared with a single tree.
Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially, with each new tree fitted to the residual errors of the ensemble so far, and usually reaches high accuracy on tabular data.
K-means clustering assigns points to the nearest of k centroids, recomputes each centroid as the mean of its points, and repeats until assignments stop changing.
Principal component analysis projects data onto orthogonal directions of maximum variance, reducing the number of dimensions while keeping most of the information.
Precision is the share of predicted positives that are correct, while recall is the share of actual positives that were found. The F1 score is their harmonic mean.
ROC AUC measures how well a classifier ranks positive examples above negative ones across all decision thresholds, and equals the chance that a random positive outscores a random negative.
Cross-validation splits the data into folds, trains on all but one fold and validates on the held-out fold, then averages the scores to estimate generalization.
Overfitting happens when a model memorizes noise in the training set, giving excellent training accuracy but poor accuracy on unseen data.
L1 and L2 regularization add a penalty on the size of the weights to the loss. L1 can zero out weights entirely, while L2 shrinks them smoothly.
Self-attention lets each token in a transformer weigh every other token in the sequence when building its representation, so the model captures long-range dependencies.
Tokenization splits raw text into subword units such as byte-pair encodings, so language models can handle rare words with a fixed vocabulary.
Word embeddings map words to dense vectors so that words used in similar contexts end up close together, which captures semantic similarity.
